evidence.claim: Independent candidate Chadchart Sittipunt won Bangkok's first governor election in nine years by a record 1.3 million votes, in a race with 31 candidates and 4.4 million eligible voters.
evidence.title: Bangkok votes in new governor for first time in nine years
evidence.excerpt: Independent candidate Chadchart Sittipunt won Bangkok's first governor election in nine years by a record 1.3 million votes, in a race with 31 candidates and 4.4 million eligible voters.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous election-result report with direct vote totals and clear context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but relevant: it shows meaningful electoral contestation under Prayut's government, not a personal action by Prayut.
contrary_evidence: It is a local race, not a national election, so it does not by itself prove national democratic openness.

evidence.claim: The Constitutional Court suspended Prayuth Chan-ocha from official duties while reviewing whether he had hit the eight-year term limit set in the 2017 constitution written by a military-appointed committee after the coup.
evidence.title: Explainer-How a Thai court suspended Prime Minister Prayuth
evidence.excerpt: The Constitutional Court suspended Prayuth Chan-ocha from official duties while reviewing whether he had hit the eight-year term limit set in the 2017 constitution written by a military-appointed committee after the coup.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous constitutional-court report with direct legal and political context.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Prayut's own tenure and the opposition petition, while also showing inherited post-coup constitutional constraints.
contrary_evidence: The suspension was temporary and came from the court, not from Prayut's own initiative.

evidence.claim: After the court suspension, Prayuth said he would continue his duties as defence minister, while Prawit Wongsuwan served as acting prime minister.
evidence.title: Suspended Thai PM Prayuth says to continue as defence minister
evidence.excerpt: After the court suspension, Prayuth said he would continue his duties as defence minister, while Prawit Wongsuwan served as acting prime minister.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters dispatch with a direct statement from Prayut and a clear caretaker arrangement.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and during the suspension window.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Prayut personally asserted ongoing defence-minister authority despite losing PM duties temporarily.
contrary_evidence: This does not prove he controlled the premiership during suspension; it shows continued influence through another office.

evidence.claim: The Constitutional Court ruled 6:3 that Prayut had not exceeded the eight-year limit because the count began on April 6, 2017, allowing him to continue as prime minister.
evidence.title: Constitutional Court rules Prayut can stay on as PM
evidence.excerpt: The Constitutional Court ruled 6:3 that Prayut had not exceeded the eight-year limit because the count began on April 6, 2017, allowing him to continue as prime minister.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local outlet reporting the formal court holding and the date-counting rationale; strong for the legal outcome, though not the court text itself.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Prayut's tenure; this is a successful legal defense of incumbency, not a democratic opening by itself.
contrary_evidence: It preserves incumbency rather than demonstrating respect for succession limits in a substantive sense.

evidence.claim: The report says self-censorship remained widespread in mainstream Thai media, but protest-era digital publishers created an alternative media system that openly criticized the government and the monarchy.
evidence.title: Thailand
evidence.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism
evidence.excerpt: The report says self-censorship remained widespread in mainstream Thai media, but protest-era digital publishers created an alternative media system that openly criticized the government and the monarchy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: University/Reuters Institute country report based on survey and expert analysis; strong for media environment, though not a legal finding.
evidence.period_fit: Published in mid-2022 and describing the 2022 information environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect: it describes the broader environment under Prayut's government rather than a single decree or personal order.
contrary_evidence: The same report indicates online and protest media had expanded, so the space was not wholly closed.

evidence.claim: The association said the culture of self-censorship lived on in 2022, even as Thailand's RSF press-freedom ranking improved to 115, because libel, lese-majeste, and Computer Crimes Act provisions continued to discourage straightforward coverage.
evidence.title: Thai Journalists Association annual media situational report for 2022
evidence.excerpt: The association said the culture of self-censorship lived on in 2022, even as Thailand's RSF press-freedom ranking improved to 115, because libel, lese-majeste, and Computer Crimes Act provisions continued to discourage straightforward coverage.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local professional association assessment with a specific ranking reference and explanation of ongoing legal chill.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but meaningful: it reflects the political environment under Prayut's government, not a single personal order.
contrary_evidence: The report notes a modest improvement in press-freedom ranking, so the environment was restrictive but not static.

evidence.claim: Thailand's government warned creators to be careful with content referencing the monarchy after a promotional video angered royalists, and the spokesman said such content could be against the law.
evidence.title: Thailand urges care over content as Lazada promotion angers royalists
evidence.excerpt: Thailand's government warned creators to be careful with content referencing the monarchy after a promotional video angered royalists, and the spokesman said such content could be against the law.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters dispatch with a direct government statement and contemporaneous event details.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct enough to the Prayut administration because the warning came from its government spokesman; not necessarily from Prayut personally.
contrary_evidence: The incident was about private content and royalist reaction, not a formal censorship order against a named opposition outlet.

evidence.claim: The 2022 military and police reshuffles were heavily shaped by political considerations, and Prayut Chan-o-cha and Prawit Wongsuwan appointed their favourites to senior army and police posts while palace influence increased.
evidence.title: Dissecting Thailand's 2022 Military and Police Reshuffles: Palace Proactivity?
evidence.excerpt: The 2022 military and police reshuffles were heavily shaped by political considerations, and Prayut Chan-o-cha and Prawit Wongsuwan appointed their favourites to senior army and police posts while palace influence increased.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Expert policy analysis from a respected regional research institute; strong on appointments and factionalization, though still interpretive.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and specifically about the appointment cycle that year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly relevant: the paper names Prayut and Prawit as appointing favourites, but also notes palace influence, so attribution is mixed and not fully personal.
contrary_evidence: The report also says palace proactivity increased, so not all influence was Prayut's.
Appointment influence does not automatically prove democratic backsliding in every dimension.

evidence.claim: Thai police fired rubber bullets to disperse an anti-APEC protest, and Reuters reported that at least 10 protesters were arrested and the protest was aimed at Prayut Chan-o-cha's ouster.
evidence.title: Thai police use rubber bullets to disperse protest over APEC summit
evidence.excerpt: Thai police fired rubber bullets to disperse an anti-APEC protest, and Reuters reported that at least 10 protesters were arrested and the protest was aimed at Prayut Chan-o-cha's ouster.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraphs of the Reuters copy
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous report with direct event details and protest context.
evidence.period_fit: Exactly in 2022 and tied to an in-country political protest.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct to the Prayut government because the protest targeted him and police action was under his administration; the immediate actors were police commanders, not Prayut personally.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes protesters clashed with police and that officers were injured, so the event was not one-sided state abuse alone.

evidence.claim: Amnesty said the 18 November APEC crackdown caused at least nine injuries among protesters and four reporters and led to 25 arrests, describing the response as violent suppression of peaceful assembly.
evidence.title: Thailand: Stop using force to crack down on APEC protests
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty said the 18 November APEC crackdown caused at least nine injuries among protesters and four reporters and led to 25 arrests, describing the response as violent suppression of peaceful assembly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct human-rights monitoring organization with specific event counts and a clear rights-based interpretation, useful as independent corroboration of Reuters.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Prayut government through the crowd-control police; direct personal orders are not shown, so responsibility is institutional and supervisory rather than purely personal.
contrary_evidence: Amnesty reports both injuries to protesters and injuries to officers, and the event involved a protest against the summit.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 ruler-attributed existential-risk choice, escalation, or crisis-management episode is shown.
Command-and-control, custody, and safety-governance evidence tied specifically to Prayut remains thin.
PM-level attribution for 2022 international-security choices is still thin; most evidence is ministry or delegation posture.
The Myanmar and Ukraine material does not yet show concrete peace or accountability outcomes attributable to Prayut.
Direct chain-of-command evidence for the APEC crackdown and the deep-south emergency regime remains limited.
The torture/disappearance law is an important reform, but year-end enforcement evidence is still weak.
Direct evidence on the sponsors and mechanism of the election-system change is still thin.
4B.4 and 4B.7 remain under-evidenced relative to the stronger protest, media, and term-limit material.
Budget intent and macro recovery are better evidenced than actual implementation and take-up.
Evidence on appointments, anti-capture, and mistake-correction is still weak.
Direct service-delivery, take-up, and quality evidence is thin outside budget allocations and national surveys.
Ruler-specific causal attribution for rural, child, and mental-health outcomes remains weak.
No independent 2022 finding of personal lying, self-dealing, or concealed conflict of interest is shown.
The package relies too much on allegations, self-defense, and broader regime context.
The program basis is only partly explicit; some objectives are inferred from budgets and coalition moves rather than a single frozen program statement.
Outcome evidence is sectoral and mixed, and external reopening effects remain hard to separate from ruler skill.
